name: FaceTite / Renuvion

card.summary: Subdermal radiofrequency (FaceTite) and helium-plasma (Renuvion) devices used to tighten the jawline and neck without a facelift; evidence is mostly case series, and the FDA has warned about off-label use.
card.note: The FDA has issued warnings about off-label Renuvion use and reported burns in adverse-event data; published studies are mainly retrospective.

quick.overview:
FaceTite and Renuvion are two different minimally invasive tightening technologies often mentioned together. FaceTite (made by InMode) places a small probe under the skin that delivers bipolar radiofrequency energy to heat fat and the underside of the skin; Renuvion (made by Apyx Medical, formerly Bovie) uses helium plasma with radiofrequency energy to heat and contract subdermal tissue.

They are used on the jawline, jowls and neck for patients with some laxity who are not ready for, or do not want, a facelift or neck lift. Published evidence is mostly retrospective reviews and case series, and no randomized trials were found among the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: Energy is delivered into the subdermal layer through small access points, heating adipose tissue and the dermis. The heat is intended to contract tissue and stimulate collagen remodeling, and the procedures are sometimes combined with liposuction or buccal fat pad removal.
quick.risks: Superficial burns, seromas, asymmetry and pigmentation changes are the most common complications described for Renuvion, with rarer infection, nerve damage and scarring. The FDA has warned against off-label use, and a 2026 surgical paper discusses fibrosis, fat loss and added complexity when patients later undergo neck lift after nonsurgical treatments.

lead: FaceTite and Renuvion are minimally invasive devices for tightening loose skin and contouring the lower face and neck. FaceTite, from InMode, delivers bipolar radiofrequency energy to the subdermal space through a small probe; Renuvion, which grew out of the J-Plasma system from Apyx Medical (formerly Bovie Medical), uses helium plasma energy to heat and contract subdermal soft tissue.[1][2][3]

They are discussed as options in what surgeons call the treatment gap: patients with laxity too severe for traditional noninvasive devices but not severe enough to justify an excisional operation.[4][5] Published studies are largely retrospective reviews and descriptive case series, often reporting FaceTite combined with fractional radiofrequency or liposuction.[4][5][6]
The FDA has cleared Renuvion for specific indications and has warned against off-label uses, citing reports of burns and tissue damage.[2]
infobox: Dermal resurfacing (May 2022); lax skin of the neck (July 2022); subcutaneous tissue contraction (Feb 2023)
Retrospective series; no randomized trials found

paras: A 2022 review of subcutaneous radiofrequency-assisted liposculpture states that FaceTite and the related AccuTite can deliver energy into the subdermal space to target dermal collagen, offering an option for skin laxity and excess adipose of the face and neck with less downtime, lower cost and fewer complications than neck lift or face and neck lift.[6]

Renuvion combines helium plasma with radiofrequency to heat and contract tissue. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports FDA clearances for the J-Plasma generator in 2009 and for expanded indications including dermal resurfacing in May 2022, improving the appearance of lax skin in the neck in July 2022, and coagulating and contracting subcutaneous soft tissue in February 2023.[2]

A 2019 paper describes combining adjustable-depth fractional radiofrequency with bipolar radiofrequency as a minimally invasive treatment for skin laxity.[4] A retrospective review published in 2020 evaluated the combination of FaceTite with fractional bipolar RF for lower face and neck laxity and describes itself as the largest evaluation to date of that combination.[5]
A 2024 paper describes integrating neck liposuction using FaceTite radiofrequency with buccal fat pad excision for facial slimming and sculpting of the neck and jawline.[7]

Grokipedia reports that superficial burns, seromas, asymmetry and pigmentation changes are the most common Renuvion complications, with infection, nerve damage, subcutaneous emphysema and scarring rarer, and that the FDA warned against off-label use for procedures such as skin resurfacing and full-body tightening where the device lacks clearance. It cites 135 adverse event reports between April 2020 and November 2023 including serious burns and bleeding.[2] Because the source is AI-generated, these figures should be checked against FDA documents.
A 2026 paper in Aesthetic Surgery Journal examined neck lift after nonsurgical treatments, describing fibrosis, fat loss and increased surgical complexity.[8]

Published human data are mostly retrospective reviews and case series. They include a 2019 paper on combined fractional and bipolar radiofrequency for skin laxity,[4] a 2020 retrospective review of multimodal radiofrequency in lower face and neck laxity,[5] a 2022 review of subcutaneous radiofrequency-assisted liposculpture in facial plastic surgery practice,[6] and a 2024 report on FaceTite with buccal fat pad excision.[7] No randomized controlled trials were found in the sources reviewed.

The procedures are placed in the hardmaxxing category of jawline and neck refinement as a lower-downtime alternative to surgery for jowls and a soft submental area. Community material on them was not included in the sources reviewed.

timeline.event: FDA 510(k) clearance for the J-Plasma generator and handpiece (per Grokipedia).[2]
Renuvion cleared for dermal resurfacing (May) and lax skin of the neck (July) (per Grokipedia).[2]
Clearance for coagulating and contracting subcutaneous soft tissue (February) (per Grokipedia).[2]
